experiences/topeka-agnes-ozman-1901/acco: Paraphrase of Parham's and Ozman's later accounts: Charles Parham had set his students to study what the Bible gave as evidence of the baptism of the Holy Spirit; they concluded it was speaking in tongues. On 1 January 1901 Agnes Ozman asked Parham to lay hands on her and began speaking what was believed to be Chinese, reportedly unable to speak English for several days. Parham and other students soon reported the same experience.
experiences/topeka-agnes-ozman-1901/cont: Parham taught that tongues were real foreign languages (xenolalia) given for end-time missions, so missionaries need not study languages; this expectation was not borne out and later Pentecostals generally reinterpreted tongues as prayer languages (glossolalia).
experiences/topeka-agnes-ozman-1901/asse: Topeka is where the 'initial evidence' doctrine was formulated; most Pentecostal histories treat it as a starting point, with Azusa Street as the decisive spread.
The failure of missionary xenolalia is cited as evidence that modern tongues are not the New Testament gift.

James Goff stresses Parham's role as the doctrinal founder of Pentecostalism; historians also note his later moral scandal (1907 arrest, charges dropped) and his racial views, which led him to denounce the interracial Azusa revival.
Studies of glossolalia (e.g. William Samarin, 1972) found it lacks the structure of natural language, while being a learnable, non-pathological religious behaviour.
experiences/topeka-agnes-ozman-1901/stor:
In the autumn of 1900 Charles Fox Parham, a 27-year-old independent Holiness preacher and faith healer, opened a small Bible school in Topeka, Kansas. It met in a rambling, unfinished mansion on the edge of town that locals called 'Stone's Folly'. Parham had grown up in Kansas, had briefly been a Methodist supply preacher, and had left denominational ministry convinced that God still healed the sick in answer to prayer. He charged no tuition; around forty students, many of them adults already in ministry, lived communally and 'by faith', with the Bible as their only textbook.

That summer Parham had travelled east to visit other Holiness centres, including Frank Sandford's community 'Shiloh' in Maine, where he heard reports of people speaking in unlearned languages. Like many in the Holiness movement he believed that a 'baptism of the Holy Spirit' was promised to believers after conversion, and he was searching for a clear, biblical sign that someone had received it. According to his own later account, in late December 1900 he set the students to study the Book of Acts on this question while he was away preaching. When he returned, he wrote, they had independently agreed that in each case in Acts the evidence was speaking in other tongues.

The school held a watch-night service on 31 December. On the evening of 1 January 1901, according to both Parham and Agnes Ozman, the 30-year-old Ozman, a former Midwest Bible-school student and city missionary, asked Parham to lay his hands on her and pray that she would receive the Spirit. She later wrote that as he prayed she began to speak in a language she did not know, and the group believed it was Chinese. Parham reported that for several days she could speak or write only in this tongue, and that she produced writing which they took to be Chinese characters.

Over the next few days Parham and a number of the other students reported the same experience. Parham later described the upper room of the school filled with students speaking what they believed were various human languages, including, they thought, Swedish, Russian, Bulgarian, Japanese and others. No linguist was present to examine these claims; the identifications were the participants' own.

Parham drew a bold conclusion. He taught that tongues were the 'initial evidence' of Spirit baptism and that the languages were real foreign tongues (later called xenolalia), given so that missionaries could preach to the nations without study in the short time left before Christ's return. Reporters from Topeka and Kansas City visited the school; some coverage was curious, some mocking. Early attempts by Parham's followers to use their tongues abroad did not produce the expected results, and later Pentecostals would generally understand tongues as prayer and praise in a language unknown to the speaker rather than as a missionary tool.

The immediate aftermath was disappointing. Parham's preaching tours drew little response, the school closed, and Stone's Folly was sold and later destroyed by fire. The movement revived in 1903 with a healing campaign in Galena, Kansas, and spread into Texas, where Parham opened a short-term school in Houston in December 1905. There a Black Holiness preacher, William J. Seymour, was allowed to listen to the lessons only from the hallway because of segregation. Seymour accepted Parham's teaching on tongues and carried it to Los Angeles in 1906.

Parham himself was soon sidelined. He broke with the Azusa Street Mission in late 1906, condemning its interracial worship and emotional excess, and in 1907 he was arrested in Texas on a morals charge that was later dropped but damaged his standing. He also promoted Anglo-Israelite ideas and, in later years, expressed sympathy for white-supremacist groups. Ozman married, joined the Assemblies of God and continued in ministry with her husband; her short memoir became a standard testimony in Pentecostal histories.

Parham opens Bethel Bible School in 'Stone's Folly', a mansion in Topeka, Kansas.

experiences/topeka-agnes-ozman-1901/sign: Topeka gave Pentecostalism its most distinctive doctrinal formula: that speaking in tongues is the 'initial evidence' of baptism in the Holy Spirit, a teaching still held by the Assemblies of God and many classical Pentecostal bodies. Because of this, many histories date the birth of Pentecostalism to 1 January 1901, although historians now stress multiple origins in India, Wales, Korea and Chile and the decisive role of Azusa Street. The episode also shows how belief can be revised in practice: the expectation of missionary xenolalia faded as tongues were reinterpreted as prayer languages. Critics, including many evangelicals and some Pentecostals, question the initial-evidence doctrine itself, and Parham's racism and later conduct remain a troubling part of the movement's founding story.
experiences/welsh-revival-1904/title: The Welsh Revival and Evan Roberts
experiences/welsh-revival-1904/account: Paraphrase of contemporary press reports (Western Mail; W.T. Stead) and Roberts' own statements: after an intense experience at Blaenannerch in September 1904, during which he prayed 'Bend me', 25-year-old former miner Evan Roberts returned home and began meetings at Moriah Chapel, Loughor, on 31 October 1904. Meetings lasted into the early morning with spontaneous prayer, hymn-singing in Welsh, confession and few sermons. Roberts urged four conditions: confess all known sin, remove anything doubtful, obey the Spirit promptly, and confess Christ publicly. Some 100,000 conversions were claimed within months; magistrates reported reduced drunkenness and crime.
experiences/welsh-revival-1904/contempor: Supporters hailed it as a modern Pentecost; critics such as Rev. Peter Price (1905) attacked Roberts as a 'sham revival' leader. Roberts claimed visions and the ability to discern hidden sin in meetings, then collapsed from exhaustion in 1906 and withdrew, later co-writing War on the Saints (1912) with Jessie Penn-Lewis, which warned of deceptive spirits.
experiences/welsh-revival-1904/assessmen: Remembered as the last great Welsh revival and a model of prayer-led, Spirit-led worship; many argue its moral fruit was real though short-lived in chapel attendance.
A direct precursor: Frank Bartleman corresponded with Roberts before Azusa Street, and many early British Pentecostal leaders (e.g. the Jeffreys brothers, Donald Gee's generation) were touched by it.
Some Reformed writers question its weak preaching and stress on immediate impressions, and point to Roberts' breakdown.
Eifion Evans and others link it to Welsh culture, the coal-mining society and pre-war religious anxiety; conversion numbers were real but chapel membership declined steadily after 1906.
experiences/welsh-revival-1904/debates/1: Roberts' claimed discernment and later breakdown.
experiences/welsh-revival-1904/story:
At the start of the twentieth century Wales was a land of chapels. Nonconformist denominations, especially the Calvinistic Methodists, Baptists and Independents, dominated religious life, and Welsh-language hymn-singing was part of everyday culture in the coal-mining valleys of the south. Yet many ministers worried that the fervour of earlier revivals, notably that of 1859, had cooled. In early 1904 a local awakening began at New Quay in Cardiganshire under the minister Joseph Jenkins, after a young woman, Florrie Evans, stood in a meeting and declared her love for Jesus; young people from New Quay began to carry the movement to other chapels.

Evan Roberts, born in 1878 in Loughor near Swansea, had gone down the pit as a boy and later trained as a blacksmith. Deeply devout, he had prayed for years for revival, and in 1904 he began preparing for the ministry at a school in Newcastle Emlyn. In late September 1904 he attended a meeting at Blaenannerch led by the evangelist Seth Joshua. According to Roberts' own account, when Joshua prayed that God would 'bend us', Roberts was overwhelmed and cried out 'Bend me'. He later described visions and an overwhelming sense of God's love in the weeks that followed, and a conviction that he must go home and speak to the young people of his own chapel.

On 31 October 1904 Roberts held a meeting at Moriah Chapel, Loughor, after the usual prayer meeting; only a handful of young people stayed. He urged them to accept four conditions: confess all known sin, put away anything doubtful, obey the Spirit promptly and confess Christ publicly. Night after night the numbers grew. Meetings ran until two or three in the morning, often without a sermon at all: people prayed aloud together, wept, confessed, and broke spontaneously into hymns. Roberts would sometimes sit silent for long periods, or walk the aisles. He was accompanied by a team of young women singers whose solos became part of the meetings.

Within weeks the movement spread through the valleys of Glamorgan and beyond, carried by Roberts' tours and by many other preachers and lay people. The Western Mail reported meetings daily and issued its reports as pamphlets; the London journalist W.T. Stead visited in December 1904 and described what he saw as a kind of spontaneous, leaderless worship. Contemporary reports told of chapels packed through the night, prayer meetings in the pits, public houses losing trade, and debts repaid. By early 1905 it was claimed that around 100,000 people had been converted, and magistrates in several districts commented on reduced drunkenness and crime. Some popular stories, such as pit ponies no longer understanding their drivers once they stopped swearing, belong to the revival's folklore.

Not everyone was persuaded. In January 1905 the Congregational minister Peter Price of Dowlais wrote to the Western Mail distinguishing what he saw as a genuine work of God in Wales from what he called a 'sham revival' centred on Roberts' personality and theatrical claims. Others were uneasy at Roberts' habit of announcing that someone present was resisting the Spirit, or at his refusal to preach in certain places. Supporters defended him vigorously. The controversy and the relentless pace began to tell on Roberts, who suffered periods of nervous exhaustion during 1905.

In 1906 Roberts withdrew from public life and went to live in Leicester with Jessie Penn-Lewis, a writer on the spiritual life, and her husband. With Penn-Lewis he later co-wrote War on the Saints (1912), which warned that believers could be deceived by evil spirits imitating the work of God, a book many read as a sober reflection on the revival's excesses. Roberts lived quietly for decades and died in Cardiff in 1951. The revival itself faded in Wales by 1906, but reports of it had already travelled to India, Korea, the United States and continental Europe.

experiences/welsh-revival-1904/significa: The Welsh Revival was the most famous revival of its day and became a template for later movements: long, unstructured meetings, lay participation, public confession, and the expectation that God could 'come down' on a congregation. News of it fed directly into the Khasi Hills revival in north-east India, the Mukti revival, the 1907 Pyongyang revival and the expectant prayer groups in Los Angeles that preceded Azusa Street, so it is often counted among the forerunners of global Pentecostalism. Historians debate its lasting effect in Wales: chapel membership rose sharply but declined again within a decade, and secularisation continued. Roberts' later warnings about spiritual deception made the revival a lasting case study in discernment between genuine renewal, emotional contagion and personality-centred enthusiasm.
